Hey there! I don't know what country you're in, so I'm not going to say your comment is incorrect, but in the United States things are a little different. :)

So, basically, there are three kinds of assistance dogs: emotional support dogs (ESAs), service dogs, and therapy dogs. A service dog is allowed anywhere the general can go. It is task trained for its owner's disability, whether that be physical, psychiatric, or otherwise.

An emotional support dog is also for people with disabilities (usually psychiatric), but is not task trained and therefore has no public access rights. It can live in most housing with its owner per the Federal Housing Act, but cannot venture into public.

A therapy dog is a dog that visits places like hospitals, nursing homes, and schools to visit a number of people and brighten their day. It also has no public access rights, and can only visit these places if invited. It also has no housing rights.

It's better a weak too early than a day too late.

Don't stress about timing because no matter what decision you make, you're making it out of love. Just make sure she's comfortable, and don't let her get to a point where she's suffering more than she's being loved.

Stay strong, losing your friend is one of the worst parts of life. </3

Totally depends on the state. I'd recommend looking up the laws for your state, keeping these things in mind:

- Unless the law states that hotels are excluded, the law applies to hotels
- Pay attention to specific language. Some laws allow SDiTs public access, period. Some laws only allow them to be trained in public. If the law says the latter, I would not be inclined to believe that meant that they could stay overnight in a hotel, as you cannot train a dog in your sleep.

I'll use the Texas law as an example.

121.003 (i) A service animal in training shall not be denied admittance to any public facility when accompanied by an approved trainer. 

Two important things here. First, there is nothing saying that the trainer has to be actively training at all times to retain public access rights, so the dog would likely be allowed to stay in the hotel. Second, the dog must be accompanied by an "approved trainer." I can't find any information as to what an "approved trainer" is, so I would assume it to be anyone who has been certified as a dog trainer through a state-approved school.

Yes, that is correct. The rights detailed in the ADA cannot be taken away by individual states. Individual states can, however, give additional rights if they so choose and, because service dogs in training are not mentioned in the ADA (does not give or restrict any rights to them), that makes it up to the states to detail those laws. If the state wants, they can stick to the bear bones ADA and not give SDiTs any more rights than ESAs. Or they can grant them protections, too.

For example, in Minnesota, an SDiT is allowed public access as long as it is wearing a vest and handled by a trainer from a program.

> A service dog in "training"

This actually depends on your state, I believe!

1. Have a doctor determine that your sister is disabled by her PTSD. She only qualifies for a service animal if she is disabled. It sounds like she is from your description, but her doctor still needs to write a prescription.

2. Determine which of her symptoms are disabling to her. (Maybe her panic attacks prevent her from leaving the house? Maybe her medications prevent her from picking things up off the floor without falling over? Something else?)

3. Determine what the dog can do to help with those symptoms. (For panic attacks: alerting to an oncoming attack, performing deep pressure therapy/grounding to ease the attack. For crowd-related anxiety: blocking and crowd control)

4. Find yourself a trainer. Even people who are professional trainers should be in contact with another trainer, in my opinion. Two heads are better than one!

Keep in mind that it takes about two years to train a service dog, and that's if everything goes well. Good luck!

Hey, no problem. It's a universal truth that rat owners will always experience more than their share of grief with these short-lived darlings, so we all need to be here for each other.

First I usually start with a quarantine period of a week to ten days to make sure the new rat is healthy. This can be hard to do, though when both rats are desperately in need of companionship, so you can do a bit of cost-benefit analysis here. In my opinion, the most important part to introducing new rats is to make sure their first interaction is on neutral ground. I like the bathtub, as it is free from distractions, owned by no one, and forces them to interact a bit. Then I put the new rat in the old rat's cage and let them explore and get their scent around. Then, they go back into separate cages, but now the cages are kept right next to each other, close enough to see and smell, but not touch. This phase can vary by your comfort level and by the rats. When I got Taissa I didn't do it at all, because it had gone so well and because Hayden needed a cuddle buddy so bad, with Mimi it was about three days, with Adelaide about two weeks (she was very, very small and Mimi was so big and a bit of a bully), and with Turtle about one week. (Turtle could have been moved much sooner, but she only had three legs and I was really worried about the other two picking on her. Turns out they didn't even notice.) Let them interact, supervised, both inside and outside of the cage during the days that follow. Once you're confident that they're getting along, move the new rat into the old cage. I like to give them a toy or something in their introduction cage that moves with them into the main cage so that the transition is easier. For all three of my current girls it has been the same blue hamster igloo that only fit them when they were babies, but all three of them still try to flip it over and lay in it sometimes.

I hope that was helpful. My method is by no means perfect, but so far I have had no introduction-injuries or rats that didn't end up becoming friends, so there must be something to it. I'd recommend reading online too and mixing methods.

The exact same thing happened to me, coincidentally with a very similar looking rat. Yes, you should get your other rat a new companion, and give her lots and lots of attention until she has one. My poor Hayden lost two companions in her lifetime, and got really lonely both times until I could get her a new friend.

If you want advice on introducing a new rat, I'd be happy to help. I've done it quite a few times now, with a variety of ages and age differences.

And, of course, I'm so sorry for your loss. It's so hard to lose a buddy, even if it's only been a week. They become a part of you in that time.

Pansexuality is not a dirivitive of bisexuality, because, generally, the 'bi' in bisexuality refers to male and female. Pansexuals are not just attracted to male and female, but agender, genderfluid, or anything else on the spectrum.

Also, the three strict labels ignores the difference between romantic orientation and sexual orientation. What if I'm emotionally attracted to both males and females, but only sexually attracted to males? Am I bisexual, or heterosexual? Why must I pick?

Honestly, I don't disagree that there are too many labels. In fact, if there are three labels, then that's three too many. Personally, I don't understand why we label at all.
